turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: I must say, Mr. Worthing, that a house in Belgrave Square, even if it is let, is a most respectable address. However, I am concerned by your casual mention of it. It seems you do not place sufficient importance on property ownership.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: I understand your concerns, Lady Bracknell. My intentions are honourable, and I assure you that I place great value on stability and respectability.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: I appreciate your assurances, Mr. Worthing, but actions speak louder than words. Can you tell me about your immediate family and your background?

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: I must confess, Lady Bracknell, that my immediate family is not extensive. My parents passed away when I was young, and I was brought up by a guardian, Mr. Thomas Cardew, in the countryside.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: I see, Mr. Worthing. The loss of one's parents at a young age is indeed unfortunate. However, I must inquire further into the circumstances of your upbringing. Can you provide more details about Mr. Cardew and your life in the countryside?

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: I lived a simple life with Mr. Cardew, Lady Bracknell. He was like a father to me, and I was grateful for his guidance and support.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Mr. Worthing, while it is commendable that you have found a guardian in Mr. Cardew, I must ask for more details. Can you elucidate your circumstances before your guardianship?

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: I understand, Lady Bracknell. Before I came to Mr. Cardew, I had no family to speak of. My early years were spent in uncertainty, but Mr. Cardew changed that and provided me with stability and education.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Mr. Worthing, I find your story rather unconventional. It is imperative that Gwendolen's husband has a clear and unblemished background. Can you provide any documentation to support your claims?

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: I am afraid I do not have any formal documentation, Lady Bracknell. Mr. Cardew was my guardian, and I have always been truthful with you about my past.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: I see. The lack of documentation is most troubling, Mr. Worthing. It appears that your background is shrouded in mystery, which does not sit well with my understanding of propriety and respectability.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: I understand your concerns, Lady Bracknell. My background may seem unconventional, but I assure you that my intentions towards Gwendolen are sincere and honorable.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Mr. Worthing, sincerity and honor are commendable, but they do not suffice in the world of high society. I must insist on more concrete evidence of your worthiness as a potential husband for Gwendolen.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: I comprehend your reservations, Lady Bracknell. I will endeavor to provide you with any evidence you require to ensure Gwendolen's happiness.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: I appreciate your efforts, Mr. Worthing, but I must have tangible proof of your standing in society. I cannot simply overlook the absence of proper documentation and the uncertainty surrounding your origins.

turns.speaker: Gwendolen
turns.text: Mother, I must insist that you do not dismiss Jack so lightly. His character and intentions are far more important than any documentation.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: My dear Gwendolen, your sentiments are touching, but they are not sufficient to alter my perspective. Mr. Worthing, I require a substantial display of social standing and respectability, not merely assertions of character.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: I understand your concerns, Lady Bracknell, and I assure you that I will do everything in my power to meet your requirements. I respect your position and wish to earn your approval.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Mr. Worthing, your assurances are commendable, but they must be substantiated by actions and concrete evidence. I cannot afford to be swayed by sentimentality.

turns.speaker: Gwendolen
turns.text: Mother, your insistence on documentation over character is unjust. I cannot marry a man who is loved and respected by all and yet is denied your approval solely because of paper.

opening.speaker: Gwendolen
opening.text: I am engaged to Mr. Worthing, mamma.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Pardon me, you are not engaged to any one. When you do become engaged to some one, I, or your father, will inform you of the fact. An engagement should come on a young girl as a surprise, pleasant or unpleasant, as the case may be. It is hardly a matter that she could be allowed to arrange for herself . . . And now I have a few questions to put to you, Mr. Worthing. While I am making these inquiries, you, Gwendolen, will wait for me below in the carriage.

opening.speaker: Gwendolen
opening.text: Mamma!

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: In the carriage, Gwendolen!

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Gwendolen, the carriage!

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: You can take a seat, Mr. Worthing.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Thank you, Lady Bracknell, I prefer standing.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: I feel bound to tell you that you are not down on my list of eligible young men, although I have the same list as the dear Duchess of Bolton has. We work together, in fact. However, I am quite ready to enter your name, should your answers be what a really affectionate mother requires. Do you smoke?

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Well, yes, I must admit I smoke.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: I am glad to hear it. A man should always have an occupation of some kind. There are far too many idle men in London as it is. How old are you?

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Twenty-nine.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: A very good age to be married at. I have always been of opinion that a man who desires to get married should know either everything or nothing. Which do you know?

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: I know nothing, Lady Bracknell.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: I am pleased to hear it. I do not approve of anything that tampers with natural ignorance. Ignorance is like a delicate exotic fruit; touch it and the bloom is gone. The whole theory of modern education is radically unsound. Fortunately in England, at any rate, education produces no effect whatsoever. If it did, it would prove a serious danger to the upper classes, and probably lead to acts of violence in Grosvenor Square. What is your income?

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Between seven and eight thousand a year.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: In land, or in investments?

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: In investments, chiefly.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: That is satisfactory. What between the duties expected of one during one’s lifetime, and the duties exacted from one after one’s death, land has ceased to be either a profit or a pleasure. It gives one position, and prevents one from keeping it up. That’s all that can be said about land.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: I have a country house with some land, of course, attached to it, about fifteen hundred acres, I believe; but I dons depend on that for my real income. In fact, as far as I can make out, the poachers are the only people who make anything out of it.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: A country house! How many bedrooms? Well, that point can be cleared up afterwards. You have a town house, I hope? A girl with a simple, unspoiled nature, like Gwendolen, could hardly be expected to reside in the country.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Well, I own a house in Belgrave Square, but it is let by the year to Lady Bloxham. Of course, I can get it back whenever I like, at six months’ notice.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bloxham? I don’t know her.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Oh, she goes about very little. She is a lady considerably advanced in years.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Ah, nowadays that is no guarantee of respectability of character. What number in Belgrave Square?
